entries.previousTitle: Illusory Truth Effect – when repeated lies start to feel like truth
entries.title: Illusory Truth Effect – when repetition makes a claim feel more true
entries.description:
The Illusory Truth Effect is the tendency for repeated claims to receive higher truth ratings than comparable new claims. The effect is well supported overall, but it is not a rule that repeating any sentence makes people believe it. A 2026 meta-analysis found a reliable average repetition effect with substantial variation across studies, and later preregistered experiments found little or no effect for social-political opinion statements.

🔍 Where’s the trap?
- News and social media – the same factual claim appears again and again, so familiarity starts to feel like evidence.
- AI answers – several outputs repeat one claim, but the apparent agreement may come from overlapping sources or the same retrieved material.
- Debate – a result about factual truth judgments is stretched into the stronger claim that repetition will make any opinion more believable.

💡 How to avoid it?
- Separate exposure count from evidence count: ten repeats can still come from one source.
- Ask whether the statement is a factual claim that can be checked or an evaluative opinion; the evidence does not support treating these as interchangeable.
- Trace repeated claims back to independent sources when accuracy matters.
- Treat familiarity as a cue to verify, not as proof that a claim is true or false.
entries.reason: The old title and copy implied that repeated falsehoods generally become believed. The broader evidence supports a robust but heterogeneous truth-judgment effect, while 2026 preregistered work on social-political opinions provides an important content boundary condition.
